# useState — immutable updates for arrays & objects

> Add, toggle, remove, reorder and sort arrays and update nested objects without mutation — and see why mutation fails.

🟢 beginner · React 16.8+ · Built-in Hooks › State & context · support: universal

**Playground:** `npm run dev` → [`#/entry/use-state-immutable-updates`](http://localhost:5173/#/entry/use-state-immutable-updates)

## Concept

Treat state as read-only: build a new array/object for every change and pass it to the setter. Copy each level on the path to the changed field; untouched branches keep their identity.

## Problem

React detects changes by reference (`Object.is`). Mutating an array and passing the same reference back does not re-render, and memoised children may show stale data indefinitely.

## When to use

- Any state that holds arrays or objects.
- Use non-mutating helpers: spread, `map`, `filter`, `slice`, `toSorted`, `toReversed`, `with`.

## When not to use

- Deeply nested, frequently edited data — flatten it, move it to `useReducer`, or use Immer (`produce`) to write "mutating" code that yields new objects.

## API

```ts
setItems((previous) => [...previous, item]); // never previous.push(item)
```

## Execution flow

1. The handler builds a new value from the previous one (updater form avoids stale reads).
2. React compares the new value with the old one by reference and re-renders when they differ.
3. Children receiving unchanged branches get the same references, so `memo` can skip them.

## Common mistakes

### Mutating then setting the same array

❌ Incorrect:

```tsx
items.push(newItem);
setItems(items);
```

Same reference → React bails out. The demo shows the change appearing only after an unrelated re-render.

✅ Correct:

```tsx
setItems((previous) => [...previous, newItem]);
```

### Shallow copy of a nested object

❌ Incorrect:

```tsx
const next = { ...settings };
next.profile.address.city = city; // mutates shared nested objects
setSettings(next);
```

Spread copies one level. `profile` and `address` are still the old objects, now mutated.

✅ Correct:

```tsx
setSettings((s) => ({
  ...s,
  profile: { ...s.profile, address: { ...s.profile.address, city } },
}));
```

### Sorting in place

❌ Incorrect:

```tsx
setItems(items.sort(compare));
```

`sort` mutates and returns the same array.

✅ Correct:

```tsx
setItems((previous) => previous.toSorted(compare));
```

## Edge cases

- Read event values before calling an updater (`const city = event.target.value`) — updaters may run later.
- Generate ids in the event handler (a ref counter or `crypto.randomUUID()`), never during render.

## Testing

The demo test adds, toggles, reorders, sorts and deletes tasks, asserts a nested update keeps sibling fields, and shows the mutation bug only rendering after a forced re-render.

- [`src/examples/built-in/state/UseStateImmutableUpdatesDemo.test.tsx`](../../src/examples/built-in/state/UseStateImmutableUpdatesDemo.test.tsx)

## Production considerations

- The React Compiler and `memo` rely on immutability; mutation silently breaks both.
- Immer is a good fit when update code becomes deeply nested spreads.
